segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Tobin Low, in for Ira Glass. You may have heard of comedian Tig Notaro, but if you're a gay person like me, you have really heard of Tig Notaro. She is what I would call gay famous, which makes the story of what happened to her so surprising. She and her wife, Stephanie, have two kids, twin boys.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: And after seven years of living in the same house with Stephanie and Tig, having their two moms tend to every meal and butt wipe, seven years of the boys telling their teachers and random whoevers that they have two moms, they're all in the car on the way to first grade one morning.

segments.speaker: Tig Notaro
segments.text: Stephanie and I were just in the front seat talking, and they were in the back seat talking, like we always do. And then Stephanie said something about us being gay. And our son, Finn, leans forward and pokes his head between us, and he says, you're gay?

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Tig Notaro
segments.text: We were obviously just as shocked as he was. We were like, uh, yeah. And he said, what's "gay"? And that was a whole other level of stunned. Oh, my gosh. How is this information only just now coming out?

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Tig's been with her wife for over a decade. And as far as they knew, they've been gay for the entirety of their children's lives. But apparently, it was news to Max and Finn.

segments.speaker: Tig Notaro
segments.text: Then I started to feel insecure, thinking, oh, my gosh, here he's lived over seven years not knowing he had gay parents. What if he's upset now? What if he doesn't like his life or his family, or he's disappointed in some way, or--

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: What's the first thing you say back to him when he asked that question?

segments.speaker: Tig Notaro
segments.text: I was saying, OK, so gay is when a boy likes a boy, or a girl likes a girl. And that would be specific to being gay.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Mm-hmm, mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Tig Notaro
segments.text: And they were just like, oh, OK.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Before Tig can say more, they're pulling up in front of the school. The car ride is only a couple minutes long. And then the kids are running out of the car, and Tig and her wife are left to wonder how their sons had possibly not seen something right in front of their faces.

segments.speaker: Tig Notaro
segments.text: And we drove away, maybe going half a mile an hour. We were so stunned. Stephanie and I glanced at each other like, what in the hell just happened?

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Do you have a moment after this comes out where you're like, oh, no, what kind of parent am I that this hasn't been discussed? Is there a part of your brain doing that?

segments.speaker: Tig Notaro
segments.text: Oh, a million percent. I mean, [LAUGHS] when there's any sort of moment-- I was going to say "moment like this," but I don't know how many moments like this I've had. I mean, I did have a similar one when they were five and I was reading them a story before bed. And Finn interrupted me and said-- they call me Mare, which is for "mother," French.

segments.speaker: Tig Notaro
segments.text: And Finn said, Mare, are you a boy or a girl? And that was when he was five. And I just stopped, and I laughed. And I said, well, what do you think I am? And he said, I think you're a boy. And I said, OK. I said, well, I am a girl. And he said, huh, OK. But you look like a boy, right? And I said, yeah, yeah. And then we just kept reading the book. And I was just laughing to myself like, oh, my gosh, my son didn't know I was a girl.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: One reason all of this was especially mystifying was that the boys, like I said, definitely knew they had two moms, were kind of proud of it.

segments.speaker: Tig Notaro
segments.text: Not like in a, "Oh, yeah, we have two moms." They're just like, "We have two moms. We have two." Also, the school they go to is very progressive and celebrates pride every year. And everyone drops their kids off in rainbows. And--

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Tig Notaro
segments.text: And it's like, I guess they didn't know what the pride was. They're just running around with rainbows on them. They're like, sure, Happy Pride.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Tig and Stephanie eventually figured out what happened. Sure, Max and Finn knew they had two moms. But Tig and Stephanie had never sat down with them to say, two moms who are married, that's what gay is. And more importantly, they never said the words, "We're gay."

segments.speaker: Tig Notaro
segments.text: It took a while for me to sort that out and understand that a wedding picture and two moms doesn't equal gay.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Right, right. And I was thinking about how when you first come out, there's a moment where you have to do this spiel a bunch to people. And then it sort of tapers off, and you just start living your life. Like, I can't remember the last time I had to sit down and have a coming out conversation with somebody.

segments.speaker: Tig Notaro
segments.text: Exactly. It has been so long since I had to come out to anybody. Anybody.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Tig Notaro
segments.text: And I would never have guessed in my own house, there were two people--

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Right. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Tig Notaro
segments.text: --that didn't-- we have three cats. I feel like they probably know we're gay.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: This stuff happens all the time. The people close to you miss something about you that seems so obvious. The truth is right in front of their face, and they don't see it.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Today on the show, we have stories of people trying to end this misunderstanding once and for all. In one, they build an actual machine to try to convince the other person. In another, they call a scientist for help. One person even tries reaching out to the federal government, which kind of works. Actually, in every case, they get a certain kind of satisfaction. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: It's This American Life. Act One, "There Will Be Blood." OK, so in this first story, a person gets so fed up with other people dismissing a thing that was happening to them that they devise a way for the other person to actually experience it firsthand. They build a machine that simulates period pain.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Maybe you've seen these videos on TikTok of people, mostly men, getting hooked up to one of these things, getting to feel for the first time what a person with a uterus goes through regularly. Aviva DeKornfeld, one of the producers on our show, got curious if this social experiment really changes anything, if men who didn't really believe their partners about what happened during their periods would be convinced by this experience.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: So she went to see it in the wild at a rodeo in Calgary known as The Stampede, where the machine was set up for anyone who might be a doubter. Here's Aviva.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: I'll admit, I came into this pretty skeptical. The idea that five minutes of manufactured cramping could somehow make men understand women better, it seemed optimistic, especially when their starting point seemed to be so basic. I asked men standing in line for the machine the question, what does a period cramp feel like? Their guesses included food poisoning, bone pain, getting kicked in the balls, a pinch, and being really full.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: More often than not, they made these guesses while standing next to their partner, who was off mic, silently shaking her head no. Either more women than I thought avoid talking about their periods with their partners, or most of these boyfriends have extremely selective hearing.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: How is your period pain?

segments.speaker: Girlfriend
segments.text: Really bad.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Really?

segments.speaker: Girlfriend
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Boyfriend
segments.text: I didn't know they hurt. What? [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: You didn't know?

segments.speaker: Boyfriend
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: You're learning right now that your girlfriend has terrible period pain?

segments.speaker: Boyfriend
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: How long have you been together?

segments.speaker: Boyfriend
segments.text: Five years.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: His girlfriend asks, what did you think was going on when I was in bed?

segments.speaker: Boyfriend
segments.text: I don't know. I thought you just wanted to sleep.

segments.speaker: Girlfriend
segments.text: Once a month?

segments.speaker: Boyfriend
segments.text: Yeah. I knew it happened. I never really asked much about it.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: This kind of ignorance is the exact motivation for Lux Perry, the person running the simulator. Lux is 31. They're sharp and funny. They first started running the simulator a couple of years ago and have since taken it all over the world.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Lux is doing all of this because period pain has been the defining factor of their life. They have severe endometriosis, which is a chronic disease where tissue that's supposed to grow inside the uterus grows outside of it, which causes all sorts of problems, including extreme pain. Lux has been to the hospital with complications over 75 times, and it took over 20 years for them to even get a diagnosis.

segments.speaker: Lux Perry
segments.text: And when, A, everyone around you is telling you that the pain that you experience is completely not real, and it's ruined your entire life, it's kind of how you end up building a simulator. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Lux isn't the only one who's done this. There are lots of period simulator videos online. But the machine people are using in those other videos only triggers a very superficial cramp, nothing like a real period. Whereas Lux had their machine modified to make the cramps more intense, with the goal of getting people to understand what period pain actually feels like.

segments.speaker: Lux Perry
segments.text: So you're going to peel them off this plastic thing. And you're going to apply them directly to your skin where your ovaries would be. So--

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: The way Lux's machine works, you place two sticky pads where your ovaries are or would be, which is lower than you think.

segments.speaker: Lux Perry
segments.text: So you want to put them as close together as possible.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Those pads are connected by wires to a handheld machine, which then triggers a cramp. The machine goes from 1 to 10. Lux says most women who have tried the machine say their normal period pain is around level 7, some a little lower, some much, much higher.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: I watched 100 people get hooked up to the machine over the course of two days. When Lux cranks the simulator up, women tend to be stoic. They calmly describe the pain they're feeling. I watched one woman on a level 10 say thoughtfully, huh, this is what it felt like when my cyst ruptured. Whereas men tend to sound more like this--

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Oh, my god. Jesus Christ. OK, enough. Enough. Fuck me. Oh, my god. Fuck. Sorry. I'm sorry that happens to you.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Whenever a guy was hooked up to the machine, women would crowd around the booth to watch. They would shout questions at the man. Would you still be able to go to work? Go out with friends?

segments.speaker: Woman 1
segments.text: Having that pain, would you go to the gym?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Oh, no, no. I wouldn't want to. I mean, I probably could, but it wouldn't be a good day.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Another woman jumps in.

segments.speaker: Woman 2
segments.text: I have to pick up kids all day. Would you think you could do that?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Probably not. I don't know. It wouldn't be fun for sure. I'd probably just want to sit, watch TV, and not really do much.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: The women badgered and heckled from the sidelines, good-naturedly, but still, oftentimes, they would lament to one another that the simulator could only simulate cramps, wishing it could somehow also trigger the headaches, back pain, hormones, acne, nausea, depression, and everything else that comes with menstruation. There seemed to be a real pleasure in watching the men writhe. A tiny bit of justice, if only for a minute.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Let me just say, I know how all this sounds so binary. I don't mean to drag us back to a time when we thought of men and women as two totally different species. And I'm not saying all men acted this way, and all women acted this other way. There are obviously exceptions, though, honestly, as far as I saw, not many.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: To be clear, most of the men I met were nice, empathetic. They clearly knew what they were supposed to say. Of course, they believe women, even if other feelings slip out sometimes.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Why do you think your girlfriend wants you to do this?

segments.speaker: Boyfriend
segments.text: I don't know how it feels. So she always whines about it. So I got to test it out and see what she's whining about. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Does "whine" feel like the right verb to you?

segments.speaker: Girlfriend
segments.text: No. No. They actually hurt. Just wait. Wait till you see--

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: At least half the men who tried the simulator did so because their girlfriend or wife was dragging them, sometimes literally, over to the booth and forcing them to try it. And Lux would have a number of couples storm off afterwards. They like to guess which couples are going to break up.

segments.speaker: Lux Perry
segments.text: Yeah, we had this couple last year. They were young-ish, maybe in their mid 20s. And she really wanted him to experience it because she had endo.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Endo, short for endometriosis.

segments.speaker: Lux Perry
segments.text: He was completely dismissive leading up to. And then when he was on the simulator, he, like, pushed through it. You can see when people are really trying to suppress the experience. And so he was really like, wouldn't say that he was in pain, and they stormed off completely pissed at each other. She was like, why would you-- why do you have to say all those things in front of people? We could hear her.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: What was he saying?

segments.speaker: Lux Perry
segments.text: Well, he was saying that she exaggerates, that it's not that bad, like that if this is what you're going through, there's no reason that you can't do the dishes, or it was, like, really offensive stuff. And it's just, sometimes, you want to say something to the girl. You're like, this guy is such an ass.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: So can this humble machine change a man's mind? Eughan and Kasia are a great test case for this question because they do not see eye to eye about her periods at all. Eughan's from South Africa. Kasia is from Poland. They're both in their early 40s, and they're the kind of couple that is always talking past one another, constantly disagreeing.

segments.speaker: Eughan
segments.text: We've been married for 14 years. We have two big kids.

segments.speaker: Kasia
segments.text: Well, not big. They're 10 and 7, but yes.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Even so, there was a real affection between them in a sort of old timey, the old ball and chain, is my spouse a real pain in the ass, kind of way.

segments.speaker: Eughan
segments.text: She wants me to stop complaining.

segments.speaker: Kasia
segments.text: Yeah, I think he thinks it's a choice we have as women when we get really cranky, and I'm like, it ain't a choice. It's what it is, and that's what it feels like.

segments.speaker: Eughan
segments.text: As long as it's the real feeling.

segments.speaker: Kasia
segments.text: But I had a history of very, very difficult cramps. He thinks I'm difficult when I'm on my period. And I'm like, come on. I mean, I've got to be, right?

segments.speaker: Eughan
segments.text: Let's see.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Eughan was actually the one who spotted the booth first and suggested they try it, which surprised Kasia. She said he's never displayed an interest in her period pain, though secretly, she wondered if he was doing it to see if she was exaggerating or at least prove his own toughness.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Eughan and Kasia get hooked up to the simulator together so they'll feel the exact same thing at the exact same time. This way, Kasia can say to Eughan, this right here, this is what my cramps feel like. While they're hooking themselves up, Eughan repeatedly tells Kasia, don't cheat. And he looks over at her to make sure she's putting the pads on in the right place.

segments.speaker: Eughan
segments.text: Where's yours?

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: You're so skeptical of her.

segments.speaker: Eughan
segments.text: She'll cheat.

segments.speaker: Kasia
segments.text: He thinks I'll cheat. Do you see what I'm dealing with?

segments.speaker: Lux Perry
segments.text: So there are 10 levels. The first four levels are just kind of like a tingling sensation. 5 is when it drops to a lower frequency and should feel more like a cramp. 7 is what most people experience. And anything over 7 would be considered painful.

segments.speaker: Eughan
segments.text: You're doing it evenly.

segments.speaker: Lux Perry
segments.text: I am. You really are skeptical.

segments.speaker: Kasia
segments.text: Right? This is all about competition.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Eughan, for some reason, seems convinced that Lux might secretly crank his machine up while leaving Kasia on a lower level. Lux walks them through the levels. They get up to a level 6.

segments.speaker: Eughan
segments.text: That can't be how it feels.

segments.speaker: Kasia
segments.text: It feels really tight.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Wait, you said it can't be how it feels?

segments.speaker: Eughan
segments.text: Never. The whole time?

segments.speaker: Kasia
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Lux Perry
segments.text: Up to seven days.

segments.speaker: Eughan
segments.text: Really?

segments.speaker: Kasia
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: The next cramp comes.

segments.speaker: Eughan
segments.text: [SCREAMS] [LAUGHS] Done. Stop.

segments.speaker: Kasia
segments.text: No, we're going to 10.

segments.speaker: Lux Perry
segments.text: You're going to stop? OK, it's off.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Lux stops Eughan's machine, but keeps Kasia's on, who's now up to a level 9. Eughan does not want to join her.

segments.speaker: Eughan
segments.text: Never do a 9. What was that? 8?

segments.speaker: Kasia
segments.text: No, you got to do 9, Eughan. Come on.

segments.speaker: Eughan
segments.text: No, no. No 9. Listen, I think this one's too high. It's like going through my stomach. I don't think that's how it can feel. Is that really how it feels? Is that how it feels, though?

segments.speaker: Kasia
segments.text: This is period pain right now. I'm feeling it really cranking up.

segments.speaker: Eughan
segments.text: Don't do mine.

segments.speaker: Kasia
segments.text: Yeah. Oh, yeah, this is a period pain. Like, it's really deep into you. That's it.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Kasia eventually convinces Eughan to get back on the machine.

segments.speaker: Kasia
segments.text: Number 9. You got to do 9.

segments.speaker: Eughan
segments.text: But quick, if I say off, you off it, huh?

segments.speaker: Kasia
segments.text: No. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Eughan
segments.text: [SCREAMS]

segments.speaker: Kasia
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Eughan
segments.text: [PANTS] It's like giving birth.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Is this like giving birth?

segments.speaker: Kasia
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Eughan
segments.text: You're doing 10 now? [SCREAMS] Is that 10? Is that 10? Is that 10? Is that on 10 now?

segments.speaker: Lux Perry
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Kasia
segments.text: Yes. That's a deep pain. Hold on. One more, and then we're done.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: You're squeezing her arm off.

segments.speaker: Kasia
segments.text: Yeah, no, he's hurting me. Yes. You know when the pain goes all the way to your back? That deep muscle pain that goes into your back? That's the period pain.

segments.speaker: Eughan
segments.text: The whole time?

segments.speaker: Kasia
segments.text: The whole time continuously, yeah.

segments.speaker: Eughan
segments.text: That's not nice, though.

segments.speaker: Kasia
segments.text: It comes in waves.

segments.speaker: Eughan
segments.text: But is that how it feels the whole time?

segments.speaker: Kasia
segments.text: That really deep pain. And it literally feels like--

segments.speaker: Eughan
segments.text: Why don't you make a scene about that?

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Do you think this will change the way that you interact with your partner?

segments.speaker: Eughan
segments.text: Definitely.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Really? In what way?

segments.speaker: Eughan
segments.text: Well, now I will ask her are you having the same vibrations as you were? It's so tough.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: So do you feel like you believe her more now?

segments.speaker: Eughan
segments.text: Definitely.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: How come you think that you had to experience the pain yourself to believe her?

segments.speaker: Eughan
segments.text: To be honest, I just thought it's like mood changes.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: You thought she was just being whiny?

segments.speaker: Eughan
segments.text: Whiny.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Eughan went from, "My wife complains too much about period pain," to asking why she didn't make more of a scene during her period over the course of five minutes. So, theoretically, mission success.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: A few days later, the longevity of Eughan's transformation was tested. He and Kasia were back at home in England, and Kasia had her period. She was sitting on the couch and told Eughan, I'm at a level 8 right now. He said, OK. He understood. Kasia told me, if you think he then got me a glass of water or a pillow or took care of me in some way, that's not the husband I have. But he acknowledged my pain, and that was new. And I appreciated it.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: I'd flown to Calgary to watch men get hooked up to the simulator to see what they'd learn about period pain. I hadn't planned on learning anything about periods myself. I already have one. I figure, I know about them. But I was shocked by how many women offhandedly mentioned going to the hospital for their period pain. At first, I wasn't sure if I was just way more ignorant about period pain than I'd realized, or if I was just in Canada, where regular people can actually afford to go to the hospital with some regularity. It was probably both.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: But there were just so many women in so much pain, so much of the time, like this woman, Gabby, with endometriosis. She's 27. She has to walk with a cane. And she's applied for disability since the pain is so debilitating. And when I met her, she was about to fly to the US to pay for her second surgery, which costs about $40,000 out of pocket. Lux walked Gabby all the way up the scale on the simulator. She got to a 9, didn't blink.

segments.speaker: Lux Perry
segments.text: OK, do you want to try a 10?

segments.speaker: Gabby
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Lux Perry
segments.text: OK, so this is a 10.

segments.speaker: Gabby
segments.text: Yeah, it's like, it feels-- then you can feel a little bit more of the almost stabbies. I'm trying to figure out what this is on my pain scale. I mean, since I'm still standing, I would say this is probably like a-- this is probably like my everyday, like a 6. Yeah, no, I could definitely function with this.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: When I tried the machine, my level was 7, average. At levels 8, 9, and 10, I couldn't even speak. I was just silently breathing through the pain. It was so much worse than my cramps. And watching Gabby casually hold a conversation at level 10, I felt like I finally emotionally understood the whole point of the machine.

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: It's easy to think that because you've experienced a piece of a thing, that you understand the entirety of it. But on the spectrum of period pain, Gabby's experience is as far from mine as mine is from the men. I felt angry that I somehow didn't know any of this before. And when I got home from Calgary, I couldn't stop talking about what I'd seen, asking everyone with the fervor of a college freshman who just learned about feminism, do you have any idea how much pain women are asked to endure?

segments.speaker: Aviva DeKornfeld
segments.text: Before this, I think a part of me felt like these guys were being kind of insensitive dummies, totally unaware of the pain of the people around them. But I guess I was basically as clueless as they were.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Aviva DeKornfeld is a producer on our show.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Act Two, "Face Your Demons." This next story is about a man who wants, more than anything in the world, to be able to see people around him accurately, which is not an easy thing to do. Our producer, Alix Spiegel, has the story.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: Love was always important to Jason Werbeloff-- probably the most important thing. As a kid growing up in South Africa, he often imagined his future partner, what the man might look, how close the two of them would be. Jason was crossing his fingers for the standard version of the love story, the one in all the movies.

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: I was looking for a soulmate, the one, the person who would understand me, and complete my life, and allow me to fully connect with them on every level, and share every detail of ourselves-- I guess a very Disney way of thinking about life.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: So it felt like good news when, at the age of 24, Jason met Marius, an artist with thick black glasses who proudly held Jason's hand in public. This was 2008, and Jason had recently graduated from university with a degree in philosophy. He was out on his own, trying to get a life and a small software business up and running. And Marius was incredibly supportive, confident that Jason would succeed at whatever it is that he tried.

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: He looked at me like I mattered. And I remember him laughing a lot. And he had a good laugh, very warm.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: But then one night, pretty early in the relationship, Jason had an experience that left him deeply shaken.

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: So I remember we were sitting at a table at a restaurant. It was outside the movies. We were going to go see a movie that night. And I remember looking at him, and I thought he was snarling at me.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: The expression on his boyfriend's face-- for a moment, Jason thought he saw a look of pure hatred. It was just a flash, but it was unnerving. It felt like Jason had seen a glimpse of something deeper, like the expression revealed some buried inner truth. Jason didn't think he'd said anything to offend his boyfriend. And there was nothing in his boyfriend's voice that was nasty or malicious. But the expression-- Marius looked like someone who clearly meant him ill.

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: I remember looking at his face and thinking, I don't want to be anywhere near this person. He feels like a stranger and like he wants to harm me, to hurt me.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: Did you say anything to him, like, why are you looking at me like that?

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: No, because I thought I must be misunderstanding. And I must just ask him enough questions to find out what he's feeling in order to understand him differently. And I started to ask him questions about how he felt about us, about what he wanted from the relationship. And he reacted in a very confused way. And that was our first fight.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: Jason eventually let it go, and the rest of the night was normal. Unfortunately, in the days and weeks that followed, those brief, menacing expressions, they continued. Jason kept catching Marius with a malicious look on his face, a kind of ghoulish snarl. Every time he saw it, he felt his heart race. The look was almost demonic.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: It wasn't all the time. And usually, the look would emerge and then disappear just as quickly, so Jason was never absolutely certain that what he thought he saw was what he saw. But still, it upset him almost every time. No matter how many times Marius told him that he was just imagining it, that Marius loved Jason and only wanted the best for him, Jason found the expressions impossible to ignore.

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: We used to fight a lot. And it always felt like we had two relationships. There was the relationship I had with him when he looked like someone I could trust and love and the relationship I had with him when he looked awful. And the relationship felt very chaotic. It was good, and it was bad. And it was good, and it was bad. It was good, and it was bad.

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: I started to research facial expressions obsessively. So I read every book I could in my university's library. There were a few.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: About facial expressions?

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: That's so interesting. Why? And what were you looking for in those books?

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: I basically wanted to be able to see a facial expression and be able to recognize what emotion was underlying it, what the person was feeling. I became obsessed with that. Because what I thought he was feeling and what he said he was feeling didn't match. So I became obsessed with working it out. What is it that's on this guy's face?

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: Marius and Jason were together for four years until, eventually, the expression problem came to a head. Jason says he remembers the exact moment. He'd come into a room where Marius was working on an art project.

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: I just hated the way he looked at me. It looked like he was looking at me with contempt. And then a few months later, we broke up. It was just that particular look. It stayed with me.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: And it wasn't only with Marius. This happened with other people, too, these flashes of apparent malice. It happened with his mother, some, though not all, of his friends, random strangers he encountered in the world. It wasn't everyone. It wasn't all the time. But it kept happening.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: So Jason started to change his patterns. He went out with friends and family much less, even created a work-life where he could spend most of his time alone. He just couldn't stand to see the terrible expressions. And they bothered him most in the context of his romantic relationships, that part of his life where he had so hoped to find unconditional love and support.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: Jason desperately wanted a healthy relationship, and so he did the typical thing that people do when they're having trouble in love-- he consulted experts, went to see therapists, one after another.

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: I put myself into therapy.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: And what did you say to the therapist, and what did they say to you about what the issue could be?

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: I said, the person I'm dating or this friend isn't someone that I can trust, isn't someone that I can feel close to. And then the second thing I would say is, what is wrong with me for feeling like that? Is it them, or is it me? But something's very wrong here. And I don't know what it is. But is it them, or is it me?

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: And what did the therapist tend to say? Was it them, or was it you?

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: They would find some story to tell about that. Like, there either was something very wrong with them, or there was something very wrong with me wanting someone who I had such discomfort around.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: This went on for 13 years, and Jason withdrew more and more. Every romantic relationship ended the same way, with a look so terrifying, Jason could no longer stand it. In fact, in one case, the look on his boyfriend's face was so disturbing, Jason made him leave that instant, literally went online, paid for an Airbnb and told him to pack.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: But then, about three years ago, Jason stumbled on the source of this problem. And understanding what it was made him think about his whole life differently. It started one day when he was on this online forum and got into a conversation with a woman named Catherine. Jason described to Catherine his experience with faces, the strange flashes he saw that haunted him for days afterwards.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: And Catherine told him that she thought she knew what his problem was. She said the name of a disorder that he'd never heard of, then told him that to figure out if he had it, he should purchase this special light, which allows the user to change the color of the light through the full color spectrum.

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: I thought she was a bit of a quack, to be honest. [CHUCKLES] I thought, she doesn't know what she's talking about. But I'll humor her and get these colored bulbs for my lights. And she said, sit in a perfectly dark room with no other light sources, and put a lamp on either side of you so there's no shadows. And look in the mirror and change the colors on the spectrum and see what you see.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: Now, when Jason was a kid and, really, all through high school, he told me he'd felt pretty good about the way that he looked. He considered himself reasonably attractive. But when he was in his mid-twenties, that started to change.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: What Jason saw when he looked in the mirror was someone whose right eye kind looked out of place and was much smaller than the other one, and he decided he wasn't very attractive. He was kind of a strange-looking guy. So anyway, Jason sits down in his bedroom and arranges the light, just like the woman said. And then he looks in the mirror.

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: And I sort of went around the color dial. And when the color was green, my eye was not smaller and to the side and higher than the other eye. It was where it should be on a symmetrical face.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: How did that make you feel?

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: I was amazed. I was like-- I was truly amazed by how I looked. And suddenly, things started to pop into place, all of a sudden, in my head. It was because I've always had-- I don't want to sound arrogant, but I've always had a lot of attention from other men.

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: And I could never understand why because I thought, I don't know what these people are seeing in me. But I'm not a pretty person. I have a really ugly face. Why are they doing this? Which would feed into a paranoia about, are they trying to use me in some way? They can't possibly be attracted to me.

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: But suddenly, under the green lights, my face was not distorted. I didn't see the face as it was before as a distortion. I thought that was reality. And I was really shocked. I felt thrown, and I couldn't stop staring.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: But then Jason turned the dial.

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: And the opposite color to green on the color wheel is red. And I took the dial all the way to red, and I stared at my face in the mirror. And my face became truly demonic. Like, I remember it was so intense, it felt like everything around my face went completely black. And the change that I'd seen in so many people over years and years and years was concentrated and magnified and crystallized on my face.

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: And I looked so terrible. And the difference between myself and the green light and the red light was so massive. It was like a terrifying experience. And I switched the light off. I couldn't look at myself for long. And I cried. I sobbed.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: It turned out that Jason had an actual neurological condition. There was a name for what was going on.

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: It's this condition called PMO, prosopometamorphopsia.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: Say it again?

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: Prosopometamorphopsia.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: That's a lot of-- a lot of vowels.

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: [LAUGHS] And it's actually worse than that because the particular kind I have is called hemi-prosopometamorphopsia.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: Not much is known about PMO. It's extremely rare. But for people with the disorder, facial features distort, melting and swelling until the expression of the person is so twisted, it looks demonic, an exaggerated snarl that, for Jason, was impossible to tell wasn't real. And sitting in that dark room, looking at his face in the mirror, suddenly the last 13 years made a certain morbid sense to Jason.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: So that was the very first time that you realized that none of this was real, that it was all just a projection?

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: Yeah. It gives me goosebumps now to think about it. It felt like the biggest thing of my whole life, bigger than anything.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: Since he found out, Jason's been working with a researcher at Dartmouth who studies this condition, a man named Brad Duchaine. And looking back, they realized that all of his symptoms started after he'd had this really bad case of mono in his early 20s, right before he started dating Marius, actually. So they think that that's what caused it. PMO seems like it can come on after an illness or trauma to the brain.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: And here's another quirk of the disorder. For some people, including Jason, the distortions are harder to notice if the person he's looking at is wearing glasses, because, apparently, glasses interrupt the typical way that a face is processed by the brain. It's an obstruction that kind of resets things. So if you wear glasses, you can look perfectly fine.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: But even knowing all this, it's obvious that it's still surprisingly hard for Jason to put aside something that he's seeing with his own eyes. Jason has literally spent months working with researchers, building a detailed understanding of his disorder and how it changes his visual experience. But still, emotionally, it's just so hard to ignore.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: Like one time, Jason and I were talking over Zoom, which is typically a little bit tough for Jason, because if he has to look directly at a face for too long, it'll distort. But fortunately, I was wearing glasses.

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: So your face is totally fine now. There's zero changes.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: Because I have glasses on?

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: Yeah. If you took them off--

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: So if I took off my glasses, then what happens?

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: So now your right eye is moving up, and it's starting to move across. OK, so now this part of your nose is getting dark and pushing in.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: The bridge of my nose.

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: This top of your nose-- yeah, it flattens into your face. And then this part of your cheek drifts out, bulges out.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: Mm-hmm. And do I look angry at you?

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: Yeah. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: And does it affect the way that you feel about me right now?

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: Yeah. I try not to let it because I know. My conscious mind knows that that's not real, but my unconscious feels the threat. And when I look at a face front on intensely for a while, my heart rate goes up. My voice catches in my throat. It just feels uncomfortable. It's not a nice experience. And I just instinctively keep looking away and back so that I don't have to see it.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: Here, let me put on my glasses. Now, I'm perfectly fine, right?

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: Perfectly fine. Yeah, yeah. In fact, for me, you're now a different person. So, I feel quite warm towards this person, but the other person, I didn't really like.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: For all those years, all those relationships, Jason had been seeing the world through a distorted lens and didn't know it. Now that he knows, Jason has developed workarounds that he didn't have before. Like when he goes out to dinner, he sits next to a person, not across from them. He also has green lights for his home. All of that has eased things. He even has a partner now. They've been together for a while.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: Do you think he's somebody that you could have the kind of relationship with that you imagined as a child?

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: Because it's hard to live with somebody or?

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: Yeah. We did live together for a while, for about six months, and it was very hard. It's not just that faces change. It's that I've built up a whole lifestyle around that where I go to sleep very late so that I'm not around people, so that I can spend a lot of time by myself. I've built up a whole way of coping with this. And living with someone really undermines a lot of that. And it was very hard for me.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: Do you think that you'll ever be able to really, really, really trust a romantic partner?

segments.speaker: Jason Werbeloff
segments.text: Not as long as I have eyes. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Alix Spiegel
segments.text: For the rest of his life, Jason will be surrounded by the faces of demons, and he says his heart will always jump when he sees them because it always, always does. But he knows he doesn't have to listen to those warnings, that the ghouls that he sees are only projections. They mean him no harm.

segments.speaker: Marie Phillips
segments.text: I don't know how this happened. We used to share everything. But lately, I feel like you've been slipping away from me and taking less and less interest in my life. segments.text: You don't want to know about how broke we got, how we resorted to selling our possessions on eBay or, rather, how I resorted to selling my mum's possessions with her permission because she still finds the internet confusing and asks me what her passwords are 50 times per day. But I got to the bottom first, and I chopped down the beanstalk with my mother's ax. And it came crashing to the ground, and the giant died.

segments.speaker: Marie Phillips
segments.text: But why would I tell you that? You'd just miss the point completely and ask some irrelevant question, like why does my mother have an ax? The thing is, though, I miss you. We used to have so much in common before you met your husband and started hanging out with his North London friends.

segments.speaker: Marie Phillips
segments.text: I remember when we were teenagers, and you ran away from home. You were living in a houseshare and working as a cleaner after school. You knew what it was like to go through tough times.

segments.speaker: Marie Phillips
segments.text: Back then, you would ask me how I am and mean it. I wish I could find the right words, the right question to remind you of that time, to bring you back to me. But instead. I take a sip from my warm white wine and say, "I'm fine. How are you? Do you ever hear from those seven dwarves?"

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Marie Phillips. She's the author of multiple books, including Gods Behaving Badly. This piece was produced by Bim Adewunmi.
